title: What a 2×2 matrix does to the plane
sub: The gray grid is the plane; the shaded cell is the unit square; arrows show where e₁ and e₂ go.

frames.caption: Rotation by 90°: R = [[0, −1], [1, 0]]. Watch the whole plane turn.

Every vector rotated 90° counterclockwise. Lengths and angles are preserved, so the shaded unit square keeps area 1 (det = 1). The blue and orange arrows are where e₁ = (1, 0) and e₂ = (0, 1) land: exactly the columns of the matrix. Grid lines stay straight, parallel and evenly spaced: that is what “linear” looks like.
Shear: H = [[1, 1], [0, 1]]. The x-axis stays put; points slide sideways in proportion to their height.

Squares became parallelograms, but area is unchanged (det = 1). The blue and orange arrows are where e₁ = (1, 0) and e₂ = (0, 1) land: exactly the columns of the matrix. Grid lines stay straight, parallel and evenly spaced: that is what “linear” looks like.
Scaling: S = [[2, 0], [0, 1.5]]. Stretch x by 2 and y by 1.5.

The unit square now has area 2 × 1.5 = 3: the determinant is the factor by which every area is scaled.
Projection onto the x-axis: P = [[1, 0], [0, 0]].

The whole plane collapsed onto one line. The square has area 0 (det = 0), and information is gone: you cannot undo this, so P has no inverse.
Reflection across the line y = x: F = [[0, 1], [1, 0]] swaps the two coordinates.

e₁ and e₂ swapped places, and the square flipped over: det = −1. A negative determinant means orientation reversed, which is why no smooth rotation-style morph can get here from the identity without passing through det = 0.
